newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast seen needing to shrug off risky image.
newsitem.headline: Mideast seen needing to shrug off risky image.

text.p: The Middle East holds promise for investors but it needs to shake off its reputation as a risky place to do business, industry officials said on Thursday.

Middle East and North Africa (MENA) Economic Conference delegates said a new open-market trend had to be paired with assurances for potential investors that their money would be safe in a place often associated with violence and instability.

"As more and more countries in the Middle East make the decision to privatise there will be greater opportunities for us in the private sector," said Ruth Harkin, president of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC).

"There is a higher degree of risk than countries in Latin America and because of the potential border closures and the violence, those are two factors which make it not really like any other place in the world," Harkin told Reuters.

OPIC, a U.S. government agency which extends financing and political risk insurance, provided $235 million to private projects in the MENA region, of its total $2.2 billion in financing worldwide, in the year ending in September, she said.
Insurance for political risk, inconvertibility, and expropriation was $16 billion, with $1 billion of it in MENA.
"American investors would like to come to this region but they need more stability," Harkin said. "It's pretty risky."
Kemal Dervis, World Bank Vice President for the Middle East and North Africa, said in a speech the World Bank was expanding activities in risk mitigation for private investors.
"This may be one of the very best ways in which the bank can help," he said.

The MENA conference, which was originally intended to integrate Arabs and Israel into a regional economy, ended three days of investment talks on Thursday with a call to implement peace deals between the Jewish state and Palestinians.
"From an investor's perspective, there is no substitute for a stable and predictable environment," Joan Spero, U.S. undersecretary of state, told a news conference.

Guglielmo Moscato, board chairman for the Italian company ENI which has projects in North Africa, Egypt and Turkey, said European countries are studying ways to lessen political risk for capital intensive energy sector investors.

"Among various initiatives, (they) proposed that the European Union creates...and with the active financial participation of the energy companies, a special guarantee mechanism to mitigate political risk for energy projects."
The message of the need to coax investors off the fence was not lost, with the Palestinian Authority announcing agreements with Germany and Britain on political risk guarantees.
